summary: Defines a MIB module with managed objects that allow management scripts to be delegated to distributed managers. It was replaced by RFC 3165.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of one boss doing everything, this lets a central manager hand small programs to helpers closer to the devices.

questions: how do you run scripts on network devices
how can a manager control scripts remotely
subtitle: A protocol for delegating management tasks to distributed managers running scripts.

tldr.problem: Networks with thousands of devices need to distribute management work to local managers closer to those devices, rather than having a single central manager trying to control everything remotely.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a MIB that lets a central manager send scripts to distributed managers, monitor their execution, and retrieve results. It supports multiple scripting languages, handles both push and pull models for script delivery, and provides lifecycle management for running scripts.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can now write and delegate management scripts to work stations distributed throughout the network, but this RFC was replaced by RFC 3165 with improvements.

today: RFC 2592 is a Proposed Standard that defines the Script MIB. It was replaced by RFC 3165, which provides updated definitions and improved support for distributed script management. The core concepts remain relevant for network management script delegation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Script MIB allows a central management station to delegate management functions to distributed managers by sending them executable scripts. A distributed manager is a network device or station that implements this MIB and can execute management scripts written in various languages.

The MIB does not assume any particular scripting language and can work with interpreted languages like Tcl, compiled languages like Java, or even native machine code if the implementation supports it. This language-independence makes it flexible for different deployment environments.

The RFC defines five main groups of management objects: language information, script management, script code transfer, launch buttons for execution, and runtime monitoring.
sections.plainLanguage: A manager can send programs written in any language to a helper device. The helper can run the program right away or store it for later.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.content:
Distributed managers are processing entities (servers, routers, or other devices) that can execute scripts and implement this MIB.

Management scripts are sets of instructions written in an executable language. Scripts can query the MIB, send SNMP requests to other agents, or perform local management tasks.

Language versions and implementations are identified separately. The MIB tracks which languages are supported, what versions are available, which vendor provides the implementation, and what revision of that implementation is running.

Language extensions add capabilities to the core language, such as libraries for sending SNMP requests or accessing the local MIB.

Launch buttons are MIB entries that define a pre-configured way to run a script, including which script to run, what arguments to pass, and how long it should be allowed to run.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper device can run different programming languages. Each language has a version number, a vendor who made it, and add-on libraries. A launch button is like pressing a shortcut button to run a program with preset instructions.

sections.title: Script Transfer and Lifecycle
sections.content:
The MIB supports two models for getting scripts to distributed managers:

The push model has the central manager send the script code directly to the distributed manager using SNMP set requests. Since SNMP message size is limited, scripts can be split into fragments sent in multiple requests.

The pull model has the central manager provide a URL (like http://server.com/scripts/monitor.tcl) and the distributed manager fetches the script itself using the protocol in the URL (HTTP, FTP, etc.).

Scripts have an administrative status (desired: enabled, disabled, or editing) and operational status (actual: retrieving, compiling, enabled, or error states). When a script is enabled, it transitions through these states as it loads and compiles. Scripts can be stored in non-volatile storage so they survive a reboot.
sections.plainLanguage: You can beam the program directly to the helper, or you can tell the helper where to download it from. The helper loads and compiles it, and you can edit it whenever you want.

sections.title: Launching and Monitoring Scripts
sections.content:
A launch button (an entry in the launch table) specifies which script to run, what arguments to pass, and execution parameters. The launch button has an owner (the manager responsible for it) and a name.

To launch a script, the central manager writes a value to the smLaunchStart object, which creates a new entry in the run table. The launch button specifies limits like the maximum number of concurrent executions and how long completed script results are kept in the table.

Each running script gets a unique run entry indexed by the launch owner, launch name, and run index. The run table tracks the script's state (initializing, executing, suspended, terminated), exit code (success or various error conditions), start and end times, and the script's result (output).

The manager can control a running script with smRunControl: abort it, suspend execution, or resume from suspension. After termination, the run entry remains in the table for a configurable time so the manager can retrieve results, then it is automatically aged out.
sections.plainLanguage: Press the launch button and the helper starts running the program. You can watch it run, see where it is now, make it pause or stop, and pick up the answer when it's done.

sections.title: MIB Structure and Error Handling
sections.content:
The Script MIB is organized into five object groups:

  • smLanguageGroup: Tables listing supported languages, versions, vendors, and language extensions.
  • smScriptGroup: Table of installed scripts with their metadata and status.
  • smCodeGroup: Table for transferring script code fragments via SNMP (push model). This group is optional.
  • smLaunchGroup: Table of pre-configured launch buttons for script execution.
  • smRunGroup: Table of currently running and recently completed scripts with results.

When a script terminates, the run table captures an exit code indicating the outcome: noError, halted (stopped by manager), lifeTimeExceeded (ran too long), noResourcesLeft, languageError, runtimeError, or securityViolation. The smRunError object contains a human-readable error message if the script fails. The MIB generates a notification (SNMP alert) whenever a script terminates abnormally.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB keeps a list of languages you can use, a list of programs you know about, a list of quick-start buttons, and a log of which programs ran and what they did. If something goes wrong, it sends you a message right away.
